meanings: (used after an attribute when it modifies a noun)
(used at the end of a declarative sentence for emphasis)

(used after a noun, verb or adjective to form a nominal expression, as in 皮革的[pi2 ge2 de5] "one made of leather" or 跑堂兒的|跑堂儿的[pao3 tang2 r5 de5] "a waiter (literally, one who runs back and forth in a restaurant)" or 新的[xin1 de5] "new one")

example.pinyin: Tā de míngzi shì Lǐ Míng.
example.fact: 的 is the most frequently used character in written Chinese, appearing more often than any other character.

etymologyHint: Represents heaven (天), earth (旦), or the number 1

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.

example.pinyin: Dìqiú zhǐ yǒu yí gè yuèliang.
example.english: The Earth has only one moon.
example.fact: Earth has exactly one natural moon, unlike some planets such as Jupiter and Saturn, which have dozens.

etymologyHint: To speak 日 directly 疋

components.note: Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.fact: Beijing has served as China's capital for most of the last several centuries.

etymologyHint: A bird flying toward the sky 一

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'

example.fact: 不 negates almost any verb or adjective in Mandarin, except 有 ('to have'), which is negated with 没 instead.

meanings: (modal particle indicating change of state, situation now)
(used with 得[de2] or 不[bu4] after a verb to express (im)possibility, as in 忘不了[wang4 bu5 liao3] "cannot forget")
etymologyHint: A child swaddled in blanklets; compare 子

components.note: Depicts a child wrapped in swaddling, related to 子 (child); the picture-meaning has nothing to do with its modern grammatical role marking a completed action or change of state.

example.fact: 了 doesn't mark past tense directly — it marks a completed action or change of state, which is why Chinese verbs don't conjugate for tense the way English verbs do.

etymologyHint: earth

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.english: The Great Wall is in northern China.
example.fact: The Great Wall of China stretches for thousands of miles across the country's northern border.

etymologyHint: The legs of a human being

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.fact: China is one of the most populous countries in the world, with a population of over one billion.

meanings: (bound form) having; with; -ful; -ed; -al (as in 有意[you3 yi4] intentional)

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.pinyin: Zhōngguó yǒu hěn duō dà shān.
example.fact: China shares Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain, on its border with Nepal.

etymologyHint: A hand 扌 holding a weapon 戈

components.note: Originally depicted a hand 扌 gripping a weapon 戈; this original meaning was later borrowed to represent the pronoun 'I/we.'

example.fact: Unlike English, Chinese pronouns like 我 don't change form between subject and object — 我 means both 'I' and 'me.'

meanings: (third-person singular) (since the early 20th century, usu. male) he; him; his
etymologyHint: An additional, "also" 也  person 亻

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 也 (also/additionally) — historically meant 'another person,' which developed into the third-person pronoun 'he/him.'

example.fact: In speech, 他 (he), 她 (she), and 它 (it) are all pronounced identically as 'tā' — the difference only shows up in writing.

meanings: (bound form) this; the (followed by a noun)
(bound form) this; these (followed by a classifier) (in this sense, commonly pr. [zhei4], esp. in Beijing)

example.fact: 这 is one of the most common demonstrative pronouns in Mandarin, meaning 'this,' and is often paired with a measure word before a noun, as in 这本书 ('this book').

meanings: used in 自個兒|自个儿[zi4 ge3 r5]
(classifier used before a noun that has no specific classifier)
etymologyHint: A tally 丨 of people 人

components.note: 丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.fact: 个 is the most common, all-purpose measure word in Mandarin, used with countless nouns when no more specific classifier applies.

meanings: plural marker for pronouns, and nouns referring to individuals
etymologyHint: people

components.note: 亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.fact: 们 turns a singular pronoun into a plural — 他 (he) becomes 他们 (they) — but it isn't freely attached to ordinary plural nouns the way English '-s' is.

etymologyHint: A line 丨 through the center of a box 口

components.note: A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 中国是一个很大的国家。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó shì yí gè hěn dà de guójiā.
example.english: China is a very large country.
example.fact: China is one of the largest countries in the world by land area.

meanings: (used as a substitute for a more specific verb)
etymologyHint: A wheat plant that has not yet borne fruit; compare 來

components.note: Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Hěn duō rén lái Zhōngguó lǚyóu.
example.english: Many people come to China to travel.
example.fact: China is one of the world's most visited countries by international tourists.

meanings: used in 上聲|上声[shang3 sheng1]
etymologyHint: One stroke on top of another; compare 下 (below)

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.english: The Great Wall is on the mountains.
example.fact: Long sections of the Great Wall were built along mountain ridges to use the natural terrain for defense.

etymologyHint: A man 人 with outstretched arms

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'

example.pinyin: Chángjiāng shì yì tiáo dà hé.
example.english: The Yangtze is a big river.
example.fact: The Yangtze River is the third-longest river in the world and the longest in Asia.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wèi nǐ zuò de.
example.fact: 为 has two pronunciations — wéi ('to act as/become') and wèi ('for the sake of,' as used here) — carrying different meanings depending on the tone.

etymologyHint: mouth

components.note: 口 (mouth) — ties to harmony as speaking together in accord
禾 (hé, grain) gives the sound — matches 和's pronunciation hé

example.fact: 和 is the most common way to say 'and' between nouns in Chinese, but unlike English, it's rarely used to connect two whole sentences.

etymologyHint: Treasure 玉 within a country's borders 囗

components.note: 囗 (a boundary/enclosure) surrounding 玉 (jade, treasure) — a country pictured as protected, valuable territory.

example.fact: China shares land borders with more countries than almost any other nation on Earth — 14 in total.

meanings: structural particle: used before a verb or adjective, linking it to preceding modifying adverbial adjunct
etymologyHint: earth

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'

example.fact: Here 地 is a grammatical particle pronounced 'de,' turning the adjective 慢慢 ('slowly') into an adverb before the verb — a different pronunciation and role from its other reading 'dì,' meaning 'earth' or 'ground.'

meanings: to leave for; to go to
to (a place); until (a time); up to (a point)
etymologyHint: arrive

components.note: 至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.fact: Beijing has served as China's capital for most of the last several centuries.

example.english: You can come to my home.
example.fact: 以 rarely appears alone in modern Mandarin — it's mostly found in two-character words like 可以 ('can') or 以后 ('after'), reflecting its classical Chinese origins.

etymologyHint: speech

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.fact: Mandarin Chinese has more native speakers than any other language in the world.

etymologyHint: day

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.fact: 时 appears in many time-related words, such as 时间 ('time') and 小时 ('hour'), reflecting its core meaning tied to time.

meanings: to want; to need; to ask for
etymologyHint: A woman 女 with hands on her waist 覀

components.note: 女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.english: I want a glass of water.
example.fact: 要 is one of the first verbs Chinese learners meet — it can mean 'to want' (as here) or 'will/going to,' depending on the sentence.

etymologyHint: specialty

components.note: 尤 (particularly/outstanding) — relates to 就's sense of approaching or arriving at a particular point
京 (jīng, capital) gives a sound close to 就's pronunciation jiù

example.fact: 就 is a flexible adverb meaning 'just,' 'then,' or 'right away' — its precise meaning shifts with context, which makes it tricky for beginners.

meanings: to go out; to come out
etymologyHint: A sprout 屮 growing out of a container 凵

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.fact: The sun always rises in the east and sets in the west, because of the direction the Earth rotates.

meanings: can; to have the skill; to know how to
to be likely to; to be sure to
etymologyHint: People 人 speaking 云

components.note: 人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'

example.fact: 会 specifically means 'know how to' (a learned skill), while a similar word 能 means 'to be able to' in a general sense — a distinction that often confuses beginners.

etymologyHint: vigorous

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud

example.fact: 可 often pairs with 以 to form 可以 ('can, may'), and alone can mean 'to approve,' as in 认可 ('to approve/recognize').

meanings: classical final particle of strong affirmation or identity
(used after a verbal or nominal expression X to indicate that X is an extreme or unexpected case) even (X)
(literary) particle having functions similar to 啊[a5]

example.fact: 也 means 'also, too' today, but in classical Chinese it was also a sentence-final particle for emphasis — a usage now mostly found in old texts.

meanings: you (informal, as opposed to courteous 您[nin2])
you (Note: In Taiwan, 妳 is used to address females, but in mainland China, it is not commonly used. Instead, 你 is used to address both males and females.)
etymologyHint: Pronoun 尔 for a person 亻

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 尔 (an old second-person pronoun) — combines to form 你, the modern word for 'you.'

example.fact: 你 is the everyday word for 'you'; a more formal, respectful version, 您 (nín), is used with elders or in polite situations.

etymologyHint: A pair 又 of hands 寸

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.fact: 对 means 'correct,' but it also means 'towards' or 'facing,' as in 对我 ('towards me') — one character carrying several related meanings.

meanings: to grow; to give birth; to produce; to be born
etymologyHint: A shoot 屮 growing in the soil 土

components.note: 屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.fact: 生 appears in many core words tied to its root meaning 'life/to grow,' such as 学生 ('student'), 医生 ('doctor'), and 出生 ('to be born').

etymologyHint: A bear's head 厶, body ⺼, and claws 匕

components.note: Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'

example.fact: 能 expresses physical or inherent ability ('to be able to'), different from 会 (a learned skill) and 可以 (permission) — three separate words where English just uses 'can.'

example.pinyin: Tā hěn gāo, érqiě hěn shuài.
example.english: He is tall, and moreover, handsome.
example.fact: 而 is a literary connector often seen in the compound 而且 ('moreover') — more common in writing and formal speech than in casual conversation.

etymologyHint: A child in a wrap, with outstretched arms but bundled legs

components.note: A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.fact: 子 attaches as a suffix to countless everyday nouns — 桌子 (table), 椅子 (chair), 房子 (house) — even though its core meaning is 'child.'
那 ('that') is the counterpart to 这 ('this') — together they form the basic pair of demonstratives every beginner learns early.

etymologyHint: A hand 寸 grabbing a shell 旦

components.note: 寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.fact: 得 is polyphonic — pronounced dé when it means 'to obtain' (as here), but de when used as a grammatical particle (like in 跑得快, 'runs fast') and děi when it means 'must.'
于 is a literary preposition rarely used alone today — it mostly survives in compounds like 关于 ('about'), 对于 ('regarding'), and 终于 ('finally').
着 is highly polyphonic — as zhe it marks an ongoing state (as here), but the same character is read zháo in 找着 ('to find successfully') and zhāo in 着火 ('to catch fire').

etymologyHint: One stroke under another; compare 上 (above)

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.english: The book is under the table.
example.fact: 下 and 上 form one of the first opposite pairs beginners learn, representing 'down' and 'up.'

etymologyHint: A nose; in China, people refer to themselves by pointing to their noses

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'

example.fact: The character's original meaning was 'nose' — pointing to one's own nose to mean 'myself' is still a common gesture in China today.

meanings: marks preceding phrase as modifier of following phrase
etymologyHint: A foot meaning "to follow"; cursive version of 止

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ de péngyou zhī yī.
example.english: He is one of my friends.
example.fact: 之 is the literary, classical version of 的 — it survives today in fixed expressions like 之一 ('one of') and 总之 ('in conclusion').

etymologyHint: A man 干 carrying grain, representing the annual harvest

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'

example.english: Chinese New Year is very important.
example.fact: Chinese New Year (the Spring Festival) is the most important traditional holiday in Chinese culture and follows the lunar calendar.

etymologyHint: walk

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — shows 过's core meaning of 'passing through' or 'crossing'
咼 (guō) gives a sound close to 过's reading guò; the simplified form 过 now uses 寸 in place of 咼, but the phonetic connection traces back to the traditional character 過

example.fact: The Yangtze River was such a major barrier that its first bridge, the Wuhan Yangtze Bridge, wasn't completed until 1957.

example.pinyin: Wǒ fā le yì tiáo duǎnxìn.
example.fact: 发 is polyphonic — as fā it means 'to send out' (as here); as fà it means 'hair,' an unrelated meaning that happens to share the same simplified character.
后 means 'after' or 'behind' today, but historically it also meant 'queen' or 'empress' — two very different meanings sharing one character.

etymologyHint: A person 亻 making something for the first time 乍

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.

example.fact: 作 appears in words tied to work or creation, like 作业 ('homework'), 作者 ('author'), and 工作 ('job').

etymologyHint: Unit of measure for farm 田 land 土

components.note: 田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.english: The book is inside the backpack.
example.fact: 里 today usually means 'inside' (家里, 'at home'), but it was originally a distance unit (roughly half a kilometer), still seen in 万里长城 ('the ten-thousand-li Great Wall').
